findings.step: ask step 3: "Now read the brown number printed on the contour line that circles the hill. Type it." (box expects 200)
findings.why: The step never says this number is a height in metres — it just says "read the brown number... Type it." The main question stem said so, but three steps in a struggling reader may have lost that thread, and this mini-box carries no unit hint at all. The sibling step in silver[4] for the same hill DOES add ", in metres", so this is an inconsistency, not a deliberate omission.
findings.fix: Add the unit cue used elsewhere in the pack: "Now read the brown number printed on the contour line that circles the hill. Type the height, in metres." Box label: "m".

findings.step: ask step 2: "Type the number printed on the thick brown loop that runs round the fell." (box expects 600)
findings.why: This problem's question is about naming a landform, not reading a height, so nothing here tells the student the loop's number is a height in metres — unlike the equivalent steps elsewhere in the pack that add ", in metres".
findings.fix: Reword to: "Type the number printed on the thick brown loop that runs round the fell, in metres." Box label: "m".

findings.step: ask step 1: "Type the northing of the horizontal grid line immediately below the Stone Arthur label." (box expects 9)
findings.why: Every other northing/easting box on this map is a two-figure number (43, 77, 88...). Here the expected answer is the single figure 9, which only makes sense if this map prints its northings with a leading zero (the line is actually labelled "09"). L14 silver[1] explicitly warns about exactly this ("ignoring any leading zero... this map's northings are printed with a leading zero"), but L13 never does — so a student reading "09" off the map has no way to know whether to type 9 or 09.
findings.fix: Add the same caveat used in L14: "Type the northing of that line — this map prints its northings with a leading zero, so 09 is typed as 9." Box label: "(figure only, drop any leading zero)".

findings.step: ask step 4: "Divide the distance along by the height up. Type the answer." (box expects 10)
findings.why: This is the step that produces the n in the "1 in n" gradient ratio, and it's the one place in the whole pack with zero unit or format framing — no "in metres", no "no unit needed", nothing linking the number back to the ratio the question asked for. A struggling student could easily write "1 in 10", or "0.1", or freeze over what kind of number 10 is supposed to represent.
findings.fix: Reword to: "Divide the distance along by the height up. Type the number that completes the ratio — this is the n in '1 in n', so no unit is needed." Box label: "(ratio figure, no unit)".

findings.step: intro: "The same points test works for both landforms, so read the direction before you name anything."
findings.why: "The same points test" refers back to the valley-vs-spur method taught in a different problem (silver[2]) that this problem never restates. A student who reaches silver[3] without just having done silver[2] hits a dangling reference at the very start — though the later steps do re-teach the rule by the end, so it's confusing rather than blocking.
findings.fix: Make the opener self-contained: "Contours bend into points wherever they cross a slope — the direction the point faces tells spurs and valleys apart. Read the direction before you name anything."

findings.step: intro: "Gradient is height gained divided by ground covered. The units you divide in are the units you answer in."
findings.why: The second sentence is compressed and abstract — a struggling reader has to do extra translation work to turn "the units you divide in are the units you answer in" into "metres divided by km gives metres per km".
findings.fix: Rewrite as: "Gradient is height gained divided by ground covered. Divide metres by kilometres and the answer comes out in metres per kilometre."

findings.step: ask step 1: "Find Castleton, the largest settlement on the extract, near the middle where the main road widens into streets. Type 1 once you have it."
findings.why: This step doesn't test anything about the map — it just asks the student to type 1 once they think they've found the village, with no real check on whether they found the right place. A struggling student may wonder what's actually being asked, or worry that "1" is a real answer they could get wrong.
findings.fix: Either drop this step, or turn it into a genuine check, e.g. "Type the number of roads that meet at Castleton."

findings.step: ask step 3: "Now read the number printed in the break in the thick ring, just above and right of the hill's name. Type it." (box expects 200)
findings.why: Same pattern as L13 bronze[0]: this is the "read the raw number" step and it drops the ", in metres" qualifier used on equivalent steps elsewhere in this pack, even though the main question already calls the number a height.
findings.fix: Reword to: "...Type the height, in metres." Box label: "m".

findings.step: ask step 4: "Check the alternative. Type the number of sides of that road that carry houses: 1 if they all sit on one side, 2 if they line both sides."
findings.why: The sentence first asks for "the number of sides... that carry houses" as if it wants a count, then immediately redefines the same box as a 1/2 code. Both framings happen to give the same digit here, but the double phrasing makes a student re-read to work out which one they're actually answering.
findings.fix: Use one framing only: "Type 1 if the houses sit on only one side of the road, or 2 if they line both sides."

findings.step: ask step 4: "Now compare their heights on the page. Type 1 if the hill is higher up the map than the village, 2 if it is lower down."
findings.why: This Map Interpretation lesson follows straight on from a Contours lesson where "height" always meant elevation in metres. Here "heights on the page" actually means north-south position — a different sense of the same word — and nothing flags the switch, risking a struggler reading "higher" as "higher elevation".
findings.fix: Avoid the word height for page position: "Now compare how far up the page each one sits. Type 1 if the hill sits further north (higher up the page) than the village, or 2 if it sits further south."

findings.step: ask step 5: "Check by turning round. Using N=1, NE=2, E=3, SE=4, S=5, SW=6, W=7, NW=8, type the number for the direction of the village from the hill."
findings.why: Eight compass codes are packed into one sentence, and the student also has to reverse the direction they just worked out (village-from-hill instead of hill-from-village). It's fully spelled out so it's answerable, but it's a lot to hold in working memory at once for a struggling reader.
findings.fix: Split across two sentences: state the code list first, then the question — e.g. "N=1, NE=2, E=3, SE=4, S=5, SW=6, W=7, NW=8. Now type the code for the direction of the village from the hill (the reverse of the direction you just found)."

findings.step: ask step 4: "Now compare the rows. Type 1 if the two are almost level on the page, 2 if one is far higher up than the other."
findings.why: Same "higher up" page-position phrasing as silver[0] step 4. The word "rows" gives more context here so it's less likely to be misread as elevation, but it repeats the same risky word choice.
findings.fix: Say "further north" or "further up the page" instead of "higher up" to keep it clearly separate from contour height.

findings.step: option 0: "The west is low, near the contour labelled 100 m, with widely spaced contours and a main road along the valley floor, while the land eastwards climbs steeply past the contour labelled 550 m"
findings.why: A single 40-plus-word sentence stacks four separate facts (height, spacing, road, opposite height) with no break beyond commas. A struggling reader has to hold all four clauses in mind at once to compare it against three much shorter distractor options.
findings.fix: Split into two sentences: "The west is low ground, close to the 100 m contour, with widely spaced contours and a road along the valley floor. The land to the east climbs steeply, past the 550 m contour."

findings.step: option 0: "It keeps to lower, gently sloping ground where the contour lines are widely spaced, rather than climbing the hill ringed by the 200 m contour"
findings.why: A single long sentence combining a positive claim with a contrastive comparison ("rather than...") — readable, but noticeably denser than the other three options.
findings.fix: Split it: "It keeps to lower, gently sloping ground where the contours are widely spaced. It does not climb the hill ringed by the 200 m contour."

findings.step: option 0: "Gently sloping valley-floor land beside a stream, with a main road running the length of the dale and higher ground rising on either side"
findings.why: A single sentence fragment (no main verb) stacking three separate pieces of evidence; a struggling reader may need to re-read it to unpack all three.
findings.fix: Turn it into a full, itemised sentence: "The village sits on gently sloping valley-floor land beside a stream. A main road runs the length of the dale, and higher ground rises on either side."

findings.step: option 0: "Square 9893: woodland shading covers roughly four fifths of it and straight tracks run through the trees, with almost no buildings"
findings.why: Combines a fraction ("four fifths"), a described map feature, and a negative claim in one sentence — more to parse than the single-fact distractors it's competing against.
findings.fix: Split into shorter clauses: "Square 9893: woodland covers most of it. Straight tracks run through the trees, and almost no buildings are drawn."
